Better error models

The first-round model treats PROSPECT’s misfit as one wavelength-independent Gaussian SD with independent bands. On Traits and Spectra, that gives posteriors that are much too narrow, and held-out transmittance predictions whose 90% intervals miss most of the data. This page diagnoses why, lays out better error models, and fits one of them (heteroskedastic + AR(1)) as a demonstration.

What the residuals look like

Three things stand out:

  1. The residuals are smooth, not noisy. The mean autocorrelation stays above 0.5 out to a lag of about 35 nm. At 1 nm sampling, 2000 bands carry the information of only a few dozen independent observations. The iid likelihood counts all 2000, so it is overconfident by roughly a factor of \(\sqrt{2000/\text{(a few dozen)}}\) in posterior SD.
  2. The residuals are mostly model error, not measurement error. For the LOPEX leaves, the RMS residual is a median of about 0× the replicate-to-replicate SD. Instrument noise is a small part of the misfit.
  3. The residuals share structure across leaves. The mean residual has features at the same wavelengths in very different leaves: the blue end below ~450 nm, the green peak and red edge, and the 1450/1940 nm water bands. These are PROSPECT-D’s structural errors, and they can be learned.

A good error model therefore needs (i) a wavelength-dependent scale, (ii) correlation between neighboring bands, and ideally (iii) a systematic component shared across leaves, kept separate from (iv) a small instrument-noise term.

Candidate error models

Write the observation as \(y(\lambda) = R(\lambda;\theta) + \delta(\lambda) + \varepsilon(\lambda)\): \(\delta\) is structured model discrepancy and \(\varepsilon\) is measurement noise. The options below run roughly from cheapest to most complete. All of them fit in any of the five backends; cost is per log-density evaluation, with \(n\approx 2000\) bands.

Model What it captures Cost Notes
A Heteroskedastic scale: \(\sigma(\lambda) = \sigma_0 + \sigma_1 R(\lambda)\), or \(\log\sigma(\lambda) = \sum_k \beta_k B_k(\lambda)\) (B-spline, random-walk prior on \(\beta\)) Wavelength-dependent magnitude \(O(n)\) The spline form is weakly identified from one spectrum; learn \(\beta\) across many leaves (C, E).
B AR(1) / Ornstein–Uhlenbeck correlation: \(z_i = \phi z_{i-1} + \sqrt{1-\phi^2}\,\eta_i\), with \(\varepsilon_i = \sigma_i z_i\) Band-to-band autocorrelation \(O(n)\), exact (tridiagonal precision, \(\log\lvert\Sigma\rvert = (n-1)\log(1-\phi^2)\)) For uneven spacing use \(\phi_i = e^{-\Delta\lambda_i/\ell}\) (exponential/Matérn-½ kernel). Demonstrated below (A + B).
B′ Smoother stationary processes (Matérn-3/2, 5/2) in state-space form Smooth residuals without AR(1)’s rough small-lag behavior \(O(n)\) via Kalman filter Same idea as B with a better-matched smoothness. Needs a Kalman-filter log-likelihood in each DSL.
C Hierarchical, wavelength-specific variance shared across a library: \(\log\sigma_\ell(\lambda) = \mu_\sigma(\lambda) + u_\ell\) Which bands PROSPECT fits poorly, learned from data \(O(n)\) per leaf Pool across leaves (and instruments) so a per-band \(\sigma\) becomes identifiable.
D Gaussian-process discrepancy (Kennedy & O’Hagan 2001): \(\delta \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_\psi)\), \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\text{inst}^2(\lambda))\) Smooth systematic misfit separated from noise \(O(nm)\) with a Hilbert-space low-rank GP (\(m\approx 30\)–\(60\) basis functions); \(O(n)\) for Markov kernels Allows nonstationarity (separate length-scales for VIS / NIR / SWIR, or input warping). \(\delta\) competes with \(\theta\), so its amplitude needs an informative prior, ideally from E. Fix \(\sigma_\text{inst}\) from replicates.
E Empirical-Bayes discrepancy from a spectral library: \(\delta \sim \mathcal N(\mu(\lambda), \Lambda\Lambda^\top + D)\) with \(k\approx 5\)–\(10\) factors Recurring structural error (mean bias and its main modes) \(O(nk^2)\) via Woodbury Fit \(\mu\), \(\Lambda\), \(D\) by inverting many leaves (e.g. all 276 ANGERS + 64 LOPEX) hierarchically, or by PCA of residuals as a quick first pass. Instrument-specific \(\mu\) absorbs sphere-vs-clip differences.
F Heavy tails: Student-\(t\) marginals or a \(t\)-process Outliers, detector-splice steps (ASD at 1000/1800 nm), specular artifacts \(O(n)\) Combine with B/D for robustness.
G Likelihood tempering by effective sample size, \(\ell(\theta)\cdot n_\text{eff}/n\) (as in PEcAnRTM::neff) Overconfidence only \(O(n)\) A quick patch: it widens posteriors but does not model the shape of the misfit or make predictive bands right. A baseline, not a solution.

Recommendation. Use E + B/D as the target model, with the A + B model below as the cheap default:

  1. Invert a large library (ANGERS + LOPEX + others) hierarchically and learn the discrepancy mean \(\mu(\lambda)\) and a low-rank covariance \(\Lambda\). Learn per-instrument noise \(D\) from replicates.
  2. For individual leaves, use the learned \(\mu\) and \(\Lambda\Lambda^\top + D\) as a fixed, informative discrepancy model. Add a leaf-specific AR(1)/Matérn term with a small amplitude for whatever the factors miss.
  3. Validate with the checks already on this site: coverage of measured traits, and coverage of held-out transmittance. Where T exists, fitting R and T jointly with correlated R/T discrepancies is the other big win.

Demonstration: heteroskedastic + AR(1) (Stan)

stan/prospect_hetero_ar1.stan replaces the iid likelihood with \(y_i = R_i + s_i z_i\), \(s_i = \sigma_0 + \sigma_1 R_i\), where \(z\) is a stationary unit-variance AR(1) process across adjacent 1 nm bands. The likelihood is exact and costs \(O(n)\). Priors: \(\sigma_0\sim\text{HalfNormal}(0.05)\), \(\sigma_1\sim\text{HalfNormal}(0.2)\), \(\phi\sim U(0,1)\).

Takeaways.

  • The estimated band-to-band correlation is very high (median \(\phi \approx\) 0.999), which confirms that the residual is a smooth process. In effect, the AR(1) model judges the spectrum to carry far less independent information than the iid model assumes.
  • For most leaves \(\phi\) is pushed against its upper bound of 1. There the stationary AR(1) is degenerating towards a random walk: the residual is smoother than any stationary AR(1) process can represent. That is direct evidence for the smoother Matérn / state-space or GP discrepancy models (B′, D). It also makes sampling harder: NUTS needs step sizes of about 0.02 and trees of depth 7–8 near the boundary.
  • Trait intervals widen a lot, and coverage of the measured traits improves accordingly. The posterior medians move too, because the AR(1) likelihood weights smooth, broad features over individual bands.
  • It predicts the held-out transmittance better, not just more cautiously: both T RMSE and T coverage improve (table above). The in-sample reflectance RMSE gets worse, because the model no longer chases every band. That is the right trade-off, since the iid fit was over-fitting structured residuals.
  • Each log-density evaluation costs about the same as iid (the extra work is \(O(n)\) arithmetic), but the posterior geometry is harder: median Stan sampling time is 2307 s vs. 363 s for iid, mostly from the deeper NUTS trees near \(\phi \to 1\).
  • What AR(1) does not fix: the discrepancy has structure that is shared across leaves (the blue mean residual above), which a stationary zero-mean process cannot represent. That is the motivation for models D and E above. The held-out transmittance check is the natural test of whether they work.
